questions.question: Let $f$ be defined on an open interval around $0$, except possibly at $0$. Which implication is valid?
options: If $f$ is defined at $0$, then $\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$ exists.
If $\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$ exists, then $f$ is defined at $0$.
If $f$ is continuous at $0$, then $\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$ exist and are equal.
If $\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$ exist (finite) and are equal, then $f$ is continuous at $0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ and $x_0\in X$. After choosing $\varepsilon>0$, what must continuity provide to ensure $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$?
options: A radius $\delta>0$ chosen separately after each nearby input $x$ is selected.
One radius $\delta>0$ that works for all $x\in X$ with $|x-x_0|<\delta$.
A radius $\delta>0$ that also controls every input outside the domain $X$.
A radius $\delta>0$ forcing every nearby domain input $x$ to equal $x_0$.

questions.question: Is the following statement correct? “If $\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)$ exists as a finite real number, then $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.”
options: No. For $f(x)=0$ when $x\neq0$ and $f(0)=1$, the limit at $0$ is $0$, but $f$ is not continuous at $0$.
Yes. For $f(x)=0$ when $x\neq0$ and $f(0)=1$, the limit at $0$ is $0$, so $f$ is continuous at $0$ even though $f(0)=1$.
Yes, as long as $f$ is defined at $x_0$: a function with a finite limit can only fail to be continuous where it is undefined.
No. For $f(x)=x$, the limit at $0$ exists and equals $0$, so by the definition $f$ cannot be continuous at $0$.

questions.question: If a function has a jump at $x_0$, what follows about its continuity there?
options: It is differentiable at $x_0$.
It has a removable discontinuity at $x_0$.
It is automatically continuous at $x_0$.
It is not continuous at $x_0$.

questions.question: Is the following statement correct? “If $|f|$ is continuous, then $f$ must be continuous.”
options: Yes, because $f=|f|$ or $f=-|f|$, and a constant multiple of a continuous function is continuous.
Yes, because $f$ and $|f|$ always have the same points of discontinuity.
No, because $|f|$ can never be continuous when $f$ takes both signs: for $f(x)=x$, $|f(x)|=|x|$ has a corner at $0$.
No. For $f(x)=1$ when $x\ge0$ and $f(x)=-1$ when $x<0$, $|f|$ is constantly $1$, but $f$ jumps at $0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ and $x_0\in X$. For continuity at $x_0$, every $\varepsilon>0$ must admit a $\delta>0$ such that which implication holds for every $x\in X$?
options: $|x-x_0|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(x_0)|>\varepsilon$
$|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\delta$ implies $|x-x_0|<\varepsilon$
$|x-x_0|<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$
$|x-x_0|>\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$

questions.question: Let $f,g\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Which of the following is not guaranteed to be a continuous function on all of $\mathbb{R}$?
options: $x\mapsto\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$
$x\mapsto f(x)-g(x)$
$x\mapsto f(x)\,g(x)$
$x\mapsto\max\{f(x),g(x)\}$

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$. Is $f$ continuous at $x_0=0$?
options: Yes: given $\varepsilon>0$, $\delta=\varepsilon^2$ works for all $x\ge0$ with $|x|<\delta$
No, because $f$ is not defined for any $x<0$ close to $0$
No, because $f$ is not differentiable at $0$
Yes: given $\varepsilon>0$, $\delta=\varepsilon$ works, since $\sqrt{x}\le x$ for $x\ge0$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ with domain $X=\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. Which statement is correct?
options: $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$, so $f$ is a continuous function
$f$ is not a continuous function, because its graph consists of two separate pieces
$f$ is continuous only on $(0,\infty)$, where its values are positive
$f$ is continuous on $X$ except at points close to $0$, where its values are unbounded

questions.question: The signum function satisfies $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=1$ for $t>0$, $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=-1$ for $t<0$. What is $\lim_{x\to0}\operatorname{sgn}(x^2)$?
options: $0$, since $x^2\to0$ and the limit moves inside: $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$
$1$, since $x^2>0$ and so $\operatorname{sgn}(x^2)=1$ for every $x\neq0$
It does not exist, because the one-sided limits of $\operatorname{sgn}$ at $0$ differ
It does not exist, because $x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(x^2)$ is not continuous at $0$

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$. A proof that $f$ is continuous at $x_0=4$ starts from $|\sqrt{x}-2|=\frac{|x-4|}{\sqrt{x}+2}$ for $x\ge0$. Which continuation gives a correct proof?
options: Since $\sqrt{x}+2\ge4$ for $x$ near $4$, $|\sqrt{x}-2|\le\frac{|x-4|}{4}$, so $\delta=4\varepsilon$ works.
Given $\delta>0$, put $\varepsilon=\delta/2$; then $|x-4|<\delta$ gives $|\sqrt{x}-2|\le\frac{|x-4|}{2}<\varepsilon$, so $f$ is continuous at $4$.
Then $|\sqrt{x}-2|<\varepsilon$ exactly when $|x-4|<\varepsilon(\sqrt{x}+2)$, so $\delta=\varepsilon(\sqrt{x}+2)$ works.
Since $\sqrt{x}+2\ge2$ for all $x\ge0$, $|\sqrt{x}-2|\le\frac{|x-4|}{2}$, so $\delta=2\varepsilon$ works.
